271.quote_or_event: “My own Self is the doer and undoer of misery and happiness; my own Self, friend and foe, according as I act well or badly.”
271.explanation: The monk tells King Srenika that no outside agent protects or condemns a person; the self itself is the author and witness of its own good and evil.
271.tie_back: Valluvar pictures the hypocrite's own bodily elements laughing at him from within; the Jain verse likewise places the true judge of conduct inside the self rather than in outward appearances.
271._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; next-best only, since Jainism has no image of the five elements as inner witnesses and this verse is about self-responsibility rather than hypocrisy.

272.quote_or_event: “One who for a long time wears a shaven crown and mortifies himself, but who is careless with regard to the vows, and neglects penance and self-control, will not be a winner in the battle (of life).”
272.explanation: Mahavira's tradition warns that a monk may keep the outward marks of asceticism for years while inwardly neglecting the vows that make it real.
272.tie_back: Valluvar asks what use a sky-high appearance of holiness is when the heart knows its own faults; this verse makes the same point about a shaven head worn over a careless inner life.
272._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a strong fit on outward form versus inner neglect, though it lacks the Kural's stress on self-knowledge of one's faults (Jacobi thinks verses 38-53 are a later addition to the lecture).

273.quote_or_event: “As the poison Kâlakûta kills him who drinks it; as a weapon cuts him who awkwardly handles it; as a Vêtâla kills him who does not lay him; so the Law harms him who mixes it up with sensuality.”
273.explanation: The text warns that taking up the monk's discipline while still giving in to the senses turns the discipline itself into a danger to the false monk.
273.tie_back: Valluvar's cow grazing in a tiger's skin is a weakling hiding sensual appetite under a fierce ascetic guise; the Jain verse condemns the same mixture of religious garb and unmastered senses.
273._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com (diacritics simplified); a reasonable fit on lacking sense-control under a religious guise, but its similes point to self-harm, not to the borrowed fierceness of the Kural's image.

274.quote_or_event: “He who has the character of a sinner, though he lays great stress on the outward signs of his calling as a means of living; he who does not control himself, though he pretends to do so; will come to grief for a long time.”
274.explanation: The verse condemns the monk who uses the outward emblems of his order, such as the broom, as a means of livelihood while living sinfully.
274.tie_back: Valluvar likens doing wrong under cover of penance to a hunter hiding behind a bush to snare birds; the Jain text condemns exactly this use of the ascetic's signs as cover for self-serving conduct.
274._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; close match on using ascetic garb as cover, without the Kural's hunting image.

275.quote_or_event: “Thus the self-willed sinner who leaves the road of the highest Ginas, who with the appetite of an osprey is desirous of pleasure, will grieve in useless sorrow.”
275.explanation: The lecture's verdict on the false monk is that his hidden craving for pleasure ends in bitter and fruitless grief.
275.tie_back: Valluvar says those who falsely claim to be free of attachment will end crying 'What have we done!'; the Jain text likewise foresees useless sorrow for the monk who hides his appetites.
275._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com ('Ginas' as printed there for Jinas); a good fit on the hypocrite's eventual grief, though it is not framed around a false claim of non-attachment.

276.quote_or_event: “A cut-throat enemy will not do him such harm as his own perversity will do him; the man without pity will feel repentance in the hour of death.”
276.explanation: Speaking of monks who break their vows, the text calls such a man pitiless and says his own perversity harms him more than any murderer could.
276.tie_back: Valluvar calls those who pose as renunciants while deceiving others the most hard-hearted of all; the Jain verse likewise labels the false monk 'without pity' and says his perversity will turn on him.
276._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a reasonable fit on the hard-heartedness of false monks, though the verse stresses harm to himself rather than his deceit of others.

277.quote_or_event: “He is empty like a clenched fist, (of no value) like an uncoined false Kârshâpana or like a piece of glass resembling turquoise, he is held lightly by men of discernment.”
277.explanation: The false monk is compared to things that look valuable but are hollow or counterfeit, which discerning people see through.
277.tie_back: Valluvar's kundri seed, bright red outside but black at the tip, matches this Jain image of coloured glass passing for a gem and a false coin passing for real money.
277._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com (diacritics simplified); a close parallel of 'looks precious, is worthless' similes, though not the same image.

278.quote_or_event: “O Brâhmanas, why do you tend the fire, and seek external purity by water? The clever ones say that external purity which you seek for, is not the right thing.”
278.explanation: The monk Harikesa tells the sacrificing priests that ritual bathing gives only outward purity, and later calls the Law his pond and celibacy his true bathing-place (12.46).
278.tie_back: Valluvar mocks those who bathe in sacred waters to hide minds full of filth; Harikesa likewise rejects water-purity in favour of inner purity.
278._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com (diacritics simplified); a near one-to-one rejection of ritual bathing as a substitute for inner purity, aimed at Brahmin priests rather than false ascetics.

279.quote_or_event: “By one's actions one becomes a Brâhmana, or a Kshattriya, or a Vaisya, or a Sûdra.”
279.explanation: Jayaghosha teaches that a person's real standing comes from conduct, not from birth or outward marks.
279.tie_back: Valluvar says to judge people by their deeds and not by appearance, as the straight arrow is cruel and the bent lute sweet; the Jain verse likewise makes deeds, not outward signs, the measure of a person.
279._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com (diacritics simplified); strong on 'judge by deeds', but it is about caste rather than appearance and lacks the arrow and lute images.

280.quote_or_event: “One does not become a Sramana by the tonsure, nor a Brâhmana by the sacred syllable ôm, nor a Muni by living in the woods, nor a Tâpasa by wearing (clothes of) Kusa-grass and bark. One becomes a Sramana by equanimity, a Brâhmana by chastity, a Muni by knowledge, and a Tâpasa by penance.”
280.explanation: Jayaghosha says that no outward sign, whether a shaven head, a sacred word or forest dress, makes someone holy; only inner virtue does.
280.tie_back: Valluvar says there is no need to shave the head or grow matted hair if one gives up what the world condemns; the Jain verse likewise denies that tonsure or ascetic dress make a renunciant.
280._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com (diacritics simplified); a near one-to-one match, notable because Jain monks themselves shave or pluck their hair, so the text is criticising its own outward sign.
